papers.title: AIM-STAGE: a self-supervised framework via adaptive interval-aware multi-kernel calibration and spectro-temporal exploration for few-shot EEG staging.
papers.abstract: Learning discriminative and generalizable representations fromelectroencephalography (EEG) signals with limited annotations remains a key challenge inautomatic sleep staging. Supervised deep models depend on large-scale expert labels, yetsleep annotation is costly and time-consuming. Existing self-supervised methods oftenunderuse EEG spectral-temporal structure and adopt fixed negative-sample strategies,which are poorly suited to the continuous transitions and ambiguous boundaries betweensleep stages. This study proposes AIM-STAGE, a self-supervised representation learningframework for limited-label EEG sleep staging. AIM-STAGE comprises threemodules. (1) Spectral-temporal exploration: maps EEG segments into the time-frequencydomain through the short-time Fourier transform (STFT), jointly extracting log-powerand cross-channel phase difference to characterize frequency-band activity and phasedynamics. (2) Local-global hybrid encoding: uses a CNN-Transformer encoder, in whichconvolutional residual modules capture local spectro-temporal patterns and a bottleneckTransformer models long-range dependencies. (3) Adaptive interval-aware multi-kernelcalibration: employs multiple Gaussian kernels and dynamic weighting to synthesizeinformative negative representations, improving view consistency and inter-sampleseparability. AIM-STAGE was evaluated on SLEEP-2013, SLEEP-2018,SHHS-D, and SHHS-H against ContraWR, DFformer, EEG2Rep, EEGPT, Superlet-MAE,and a supervised baseline across 1% to 15% labels. Accuracy improved from 88.67% to92.04% on SLEEP-2013, and AIM-STAGE outperformed all baselines on all four datasetswith higher kappa, macro-F1, and balanced accuracy, including on the pathologicalSHHS-D cohort. Ablation confirmed the contributions of the bottleneck Transformer,positional embeddings, physiology-informed augmentation, and calibration loss. Per-stageanalysis showed that N1 is the most difficult stage, with F1 ranging from 0.003 to 0.046,and adding EOG and EMG markedly improved its precision, recall, and F1. AIM-STAGE offers an interpretable and label-efficient self-supervised solution for EEGsleep staging, improving robustness and stage discriminability under scarce-labelconditions while reducing dependence on manual annotation.&#xD.

ai.reason: Directly targets core interest in few-shot sleep staging with spectral-temporal self-supervised representation learning and label-efficient calibration.
ai.summary: Proposes AIM-STAGE, a self-supervised representation learning framework combining STFT spectro-temporal exploration, a CNN-Transformer encoder, and adaptive interval-aware multi-kernel calibration for few-shot EEG sleep staging. It improved accuracy from 88.67% to 92.04% on SLEEP-2013 and outperformed six baselines on all four datasets (kappa, macro-F1, balanced accuracy), with N1 remaining the hardest stage (F1 0.003-0.046).

papers.title: Anti-correlation time-frequency synergy and dual-granularity fusion for sleep stage classification.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep stage classification is crucial for diagnosing sleep disorders and evaluating sleep quality. Single-channel EEG sleep staging using central electrodes has garnered significant interest due to its ability to detect a higher number of sleep spindles and its cost-effectiveness. Nevertheless, several challenges remain, such as the neglect of interdependencies among features, reduced model sensitivity to the dispersion across features, potential information leakage during the learning of transition rules, and class imbalance. To address these challenges, this study specifically designs an automatic sleep staging network based on single-channel EEG. The network incorporates a multi-branch feature extraction module, which captures negatively correlated frequency features that exhibit significant variations during sleep transitions and promotes synergistic complementarity. Furthermore, a dual-granularity residual attention mechanism is employed to perform adaptive fusion along both temporal and channel dimensions based on statistical measures such as the mean and standard deviation. The causal transition-aware network ensures temporal consistency while facilitating effective learning of transition rules. The focal loss function is utilized to counteract class imbalance. Experiments on SleepEDF-20, SleepEDF-78 and SHHS datasets show that our method achieves the best performance with overall accuracy of 87.0%, 83.4% and 84.5%, respectively. For N1 stage classification which is more challenging, it reaches an accuracy of 57.5%, 52.5% and 49.3% on three datasets, respectively. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and its certain advantages over existing methods.

ai.reason: Directly addresses automatic sleep staging with single-channel EEG, spectral feature fusion and transition-aware design relevant to lightweight transferable staging.
ai.summary: Develops a single-channel EEG sleep staging network using a multi-branch module for anti-correlated frequency features, dual-granularity residual attention fusion, causal transition-aware learning, and focal loss. It reached overall accuracies of 87.0%, 83.4%, and 84.5% on SleepEDF-20, SleepEDF-78, and SHHS, respectively, including N1 accuracies of 57.5%, 52.5%, and 49.3%.

papers.title: Thalamic stereo-EEG detects sleep stages N2 and N3 with discrimination approaching scalp EEG
papers.abstract: Sleep and epilepsy interact strongly during sleep stages N2 and N3, when synchronization of brain rhythms is increased. Sleep staging relies on scalp EEG, which is often absent or incomplete during stereo-EEG monitoring and unavailable from implanted devices, while thalamic leads are increasingly implanted for epilepsy neuromodulation. Given the role of the thalamus in spindle generation and slow oscillation dynamics, we hypothesized that thalamic channels would identify N2 and N3 (N2+N3) better than other intracranial sites. We analyzed 477 h of stereo-EEG with simultaneous scalp EEG from six adults, including 46 thalamic bipolar channels on 11 electrodes. Two classifiers were evaluated on identical channels: a random forest with hidden Markov decoding (RF + HMM) trained leave-one-participant-out, and the pretrained SleepSEEG algorithm developed without thalamic channels. The primary endpoint was discrimination of N2+N3 from other stages as classified from scalp EEG by a sleep expert. Among regions sampled in all participants, thalamic channels performed best (area under the curve [AUC] 0.94 with RF + HMM and 0.93 with SleepSEEG across whole recordings; 0.88 and 0.86 at night). With RF + HMM, thalamic channels outperformed mesial temporal and temporal neocortical channels in all six participants across whole recordings. The advantage persisted against channel-count-matched subsets and a white-matter control with both classifiers. Individual thalamic electrodes reached AUCs of 0.79-0.99 with RF + HMM (10 of 11 at least 0.89). These offline findings support thalamic N2+N3 detection and motivate real-time evaluation for sleep-targeted neuromodulation.

ai.reason: Highly relevant sleep-staging study comparing transferable classifiers across recording systems (thalamic sEEG vs scalp), informs normalization and generalization.
ai.summary: Analyzed 477 h of simultaneous stereo-EEG and scalp EEG from six adults to test whether thalamic channels identify N2+N3 sleep better than other intracranial sites, using a random forest with HMM decoding and the pretrained SleepSEEG classifier. Thalamic channels performed best among regions sampled in all participants (AUC 0.94 with RF+HMM and 0.93 with SleepSEEG), supporting thalamic N2+N3 detection for sleep-targeted neuromodulation.

papers.title: Dynamics of Sleep Architecture and Nocturnal Oxygen Saturation During Acclimatization at Intermediate Altitude: A Longitudinal Observational Study in Elite Athletes.
papers.abstract: Athletes typically undergo training camps living and sleeping at intermediate altitudes (1500-2500 m). Hypoxia reshapes sleep through central circuits regulating arousal, chemoreflex gain and sympathetic outflow. However, the relationship between peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) and sleep architecture and how it co-evolves during acclimatization, is unclear. We tested whether SpO2 differs across sleep stages at intermediate altitude and whether its recovery is stage specific. Seventeen mogul-ski athletes (seven women) travelled from Montréal (Canada) to Tignes (France) for a 2-week altitude training camp (AltitudeCamp; 2100 m) in June 2025. During the first week (6 nights) and the last night of AltitudeCamp, athletes were provided with a validated ring pulse oximeter and an electroencephalography (EEG) headband. We evaluated the changes in sleep stage distribution across successive nights, scored on 30-second epochs and synchronized with oximetry data. Model estimates are reported as mean ± Standard Error (SE), raw data as mean ± Standard Deviation (SD). Average total sleep time was 429 ± 47 min (mean ± SD) and did not change during AltitudeCamp (p = 0.939). Across the first week, %N3 decreased logarithmically (β = -2.35 ± 0.72%/ln (night), p = 0.002) and %Rapid eye movement sleep (REM) increased logarithmically (β = 3.13 ± 0.88%/ln (night), p < 0.001), with no changes in %Wake, %N1, or %N2. SpO2 was lower during AltitudeCamp (95.2 ± 0.3%) than measures obtained in normoxia (98 ± 0.4%; p < 0.001), and overnight heart rate (HR) was 7 ± 2 beats per minute (bpm) higher than the habitual 58 ± 3 bpm observed in normoxia (p = 0.005). Wake SpO2 increased by 0.13 ± 0.01 percentage points per night (p < 0.001), with faster recovery in N1 (0.19 ± 0.02 percentage points/night; p = 0.006) and REM (0.23 ± 0.01 percentage points/night; p < 0.001), while N2 and N3 did not differ from Wake. HR declined by 0.79 bpm/night during Wake, similar to N3 (p = 0.26), but larger than the decline in N1 (p = 0.024) and REM (p < 0.001). In N2, HR did not evolve during the first week at altitude. At intermediate altitude, nocturnal SpO2 and HR show sleep-stage-specific dynamics that mirror central ventilatory and autonomic adaptation to hypoxia. Our data suggest that acclimatization is not uniform across sleep stages, and that the first 2 nights after ascent may capture the most rapid adjustments despite similar total sleep duration. Sleep therefore offers a heterogeneous and ecologically valid index of central nervous system (CNS) acclimatization, which can be monitored longitudinally with wearable EEG-oximetry.

ai.reason: Directly relevant longitudinal sleep staging with wearable EEG/oximetry in athletes, including synchronized automated-style epoch scoring and state dynamics across nights.
ai.summary: Longitudinally tracked nocturnal sleep architecture and oxygen saturation with wearable EEG and ring oximetry in 17 elite athletes across a 2-week intermediate-altitude training camp (2100 m). Over the first week %N3 decreased and %REM increased logarithmically, with sleep-stage-specific SpO2 recovery and heart-rate dynamics indicating non-uniform acclimatization across sleep stages.

papers.title: A Bayesian Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg Model for Real-Time EEG Phase Estimation
papers.abstract: Real-time phase estimation on stimulus-aligned transient EEG is critical for closed-loop neuromodulation systems targeting the theta-band, yet most real-time phase estimation methods have been developed and validated on resting-state, high-fidelity signals in the alpha band. Recent work has pursued deep learning architectures, while individualized classical bandpass filter tuning remains underexplored. This study characterizes the spectral and temporal properties of non-anticipative bandpass filtering and demonstrates the performance gains achieved through individualized tuning. We present a Bayesian-Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg (BOB) model evaluated on EEG recorded during peripheral vibrotactile stimulation of the left median nerve (theta, N=20 healthy subjects) and on resting-state recordings from the Max Planck Institute's LEMON dataset (alpha, N=20 healthy subjects). BOB was benchmarked against the Deep Dual-Branch Complex Neural Network (DBCNN), EEG Phase Prediction Network (EPN), Phastimate, and Phase Estimation with Autoregressive Padding (PEAP) under matched testing conditions: channel selection, individualized optimization, evaluation time points, and an offline reference phase obtained through zero-phase filtering and the Hilbert transform. Under these testing conditions, BOB achieved matched or better performance than these models at a fraction of the calibration time.

ai.reason: CPU-friendly classical filter/AR method with individual calibration and benchmarking vs deep models—highly transferable to real-time time-series analysis.
ai.summary: Presents the Bayesian-Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg (BOB) model for real-time EEG phase estimation on theta-band stimulus-aligned and alpha-band resting-state signals, benchmarked against DBCNN, EPN, Phastimate, and PEAP. Under matched testing conditions BOB matched or exceeded these deep learning models while requiring a fraction of the calibration time.

papers.title: NeuralFieldManifold: Uncovering the Manifold Geometry of Local Field Potentials
papers.abstract: Manifold geometry has become a powerful framework for understanding how the brain organizes high-dimensional neural activity into compact, interpretable structure. To date, however, most theoretical and methodological advances in neural manifold analysis have focused on spiking activity, leaving unresolved a fundamental question: What are the geometric principles governing the dynamics of local field potentials (LFPs); population level signals reflecting integrated subthreshold and suprathreshold neural activity that are broadly integral to clinical and brain-computer interface settings. Here, we establish, analytically and empirically, that the lag-embedded dynamics of LFP signals lie on a low-dimensional K-torus, where K directly relates to sustained oscillatory modes present in the signal. Modeling LFPs as bounded autoregressive processes, we show that each oscillatory component contributes an independent circular degree of freedom, while aperiodic 1/f structure and noise contribute only geometric thickness around the manifold without altering its topology. To apply this theory to real nonstationary recordings, we introduce DeepLagField, a physics-informed network that jointly estimates time-varying AR structure and effective model order, with formal guarantees that local toroidal geometry is preserved despite non-stationary nature of neuronal processes. Persistent homology analysis on real recordings reveals topological signatures consistent with the predicted toroidal Betti numbers in primate V1 LFP, rodent hippocampal LFP, and mouse cortical EEG, with varying degrees of agreement across recordings and temporal windows. Crucially, decoding analyses across three distinct neural datasets demonstrate that these geometric structures are not merely descriptive but capture behaviorally relevant information rivaling conventional spectral features. Together, these findings establish a theoretically grounded and empirically validated geometric framework for neural field analysis, extending the manifold perspective beyond spiking activity and offering a complementary language to spectral analysis for understanding and translating population dynamics across neural modalities.

ai.reason: Manifold/dynamical modeling of LFPs with oscillatory mode theory and a physics-informed model; highly relevant to state-space, interpretable neural time-series methods transferable to sleep analysis.
ai.summary: Analytically and empirically shows that lag-embedded local field potential dynamics lie on a low-dimensional K-torus, with each sustained oscillatory mode contributing an independent circular degree of freedom while aperiodic 1/f structure and noise add only geometric thickness. The authors introduce DeepLagField, a physics-informed network for nonstationary recordings, and report persistent homology signatures consistent with predicted toroidal Betti numbers in primate V1, rodent hippocampal, and mouse cortical EEG data, with decoding performance rivaling conventional spectral features.

papers.title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence for Sleep: Integrating Multichannel Signals for Comprehensive Assessment.
papers.abstract: Sleep medicine generates rich, multimodal physiologic data that has traditionally been reduced to summary metrics through labor-intensive manual interpretation. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, is transforming the field by enabling scalable, reproducible, and integrated analysis of polysomnographic signals. This review examines 5 interrelated frontiers of multimodal AI in sleep medicine: foundation models pre-trained on diverse biosignal datasets that may unify analysis across devices and populations; automated sleep staging systems that match individual expert reliability; AI-driven respiratory analysis that moves beyond the Apnea-Hypopnea Index toward continuous, endotype-level characterization of sleep-disordered breathing; AI-derived sleep biomarkers, including electroencephalography microstructure, brain age.

ai.reason: Review of foundation models and automated staging across signals—strongly relevant background for generalizable, multimodal sleep analysis.
ai.summary: This review examines five frontiers of multimodal AI in sleep medicine: foundation models for biosignal analysis, automated sleep staging matching expert reliability, AI-driven respiratory analysis for endotype-level characterization, AI-derived sleep biomarkers from EEG microstructure and brain age, and integration challenges. It emphasizes the potential of deep learning to enable scalable, reproducible polysomnographic analysis.

papers.title: A Lightweight EEG-Based Alzheimer's Disease Detection Framework on an Edge-Computing Platform Toward Future Intelligent Digital Twin Systems.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progresses slowly through several stages until the patient reaches full cognitive decline. The electroencephalography (EEG) alterations associated with AD often emerge before symptom onset, suggesting that accessible and repeated EEG-based assessment could facilitate earlier detection and longitudinal monitoring. However, this type of assessment requires an AD detection model operating on edge-computing platforms within the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT). At present, many existing AD detection models rely on complex deep learning architectures with numerous parameters, which significantly limit their practicality for on-edge deployment. We propose an on-edge AD detection framework comprising a lightweight dilated hybrid deep learning (DHDL) model with a channel selection approach to reduce the computational and power demands on the evaluated edge-computing platform. A key architectural component is the inclusion of dual-granularity dilated temporal convolutions. This method expands the receptive field at two scales to capture both short- and long-term temporal features from EEG signals without increasing the number of parameters. Subsequently, several hybrid lightweight layers extract distinct temporal and spatial features and are integrated with attention mechanisms. Additionally, our channel selection approach first forms an initial subset of EEG channels guided by individual channel classification accuracy, and then iteratively refines the selected channels using hill-climbing optimization. Here, we evaluated our framework on two publicly available EEG datasets recorded for the same group of subjects (n = 48 subjects): a conventional closed-eye (CE) dataset and a more challenging open-eye (OE) dataset. Validation followed a subject-independent Leave-2-Subjects-Out (L2SO) cross-validation protocol. Real-time deployment was tested on an edge-computing platform. The proposed framework achieved 92.56% accuracy for the CE dataset and 75.15% accuracy for the OE dataset. Inference required 10.45 ms and 8.23 ms per segment for the CE and OE datasets, respectively, and consumed 9.69 mJ and 6.95 mJ of energy per segment, respectively. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed framework as a real-time, on-edge inference module for AD detection. Although a complete intelligent digital twin system is not implemented in this work, the proposed framework can serve as an inference component for future digital twin systems, supporting early AD detection and progression monitoring.

ai.reason: Edge-deployable lightweight dilated CNN with channel selection matches interest in efficient, CPU/edge-friendly EEG pipelines, though clinical AD target.
ai.summary: The authors propose a lightweight dilated hybrid deep learning framework with channel selection for EEG-based Alzheimer's disease detection on edge-computing platforms. It achieved 92.56% accuracy on a closed-eye dataset and 75.15% on an open-eye dataset, with inference times of 10.45 ms and 8.23 ms per segment and energy consumption of 9.69 mJ and 6.95 mJ, respectively, demonstrating feasibility for real-time on-edge AD detection.

papers.title: Automated Sleep Staging: Are Algorithms Ready for the Clinic?
papers.abstract: Sleep staging is an important tool to diagnose sleep disorders but can be a time-intensive process. The development of artificial intelligence-based automated sleep staging programs can alleviate barriers to scoring by improving efficiency and achieving standardized results. However, careful implementation of these programs is needed to ensure appropriate use. Artificial intelligence models can generate unreliable clinical results if models are not trained on heterogenous data that represent both common and infrequent sleep disorders. It is essential to recognize the limitations of artificial intelligence-based scoring prior to integration in clinical workflows to promote meaningful improvements in care delivery.

ai.topic: Clinical readiness of automated sleep staging
ai.reason: Review on deployment, heterogeneity and limitations of automated staging—useful framing for generalizable, reproducible staging algorithms.
ai.summary: This review discusses the development and clinical implementation of AI-based automated sleep staging programs, noting their potential to improve efficiency and standardization but warning that models trained on non-heterogeneous data may yield unreliable results. It stresses the need to recognize limitations before integrating AI scoring into clinical workflows.

papers.title: SafeLens: A Statistically Controlled Nonlinear Machine Learning Framework for Characterizing Hidden Dynamics in Event-Locked Neural Activity
papers.abstract: Machine learning has advanced rapidly over the past decade, yet event-locked neural activity is still analyzed predominantly with traditional statistics and linear models. While traditional linear methods provide computationally tractable statistical control for pre-selected features or trial-averaged waveforms, they miss subtle nonlinear and trial-varying neural dynamics. Nonlinear models can capture these complex patterns, but their feature reliance is opaque and notoriously difficult to threshold statistically. We introduce SafeLens (Searchlight Analysis of Fluctuation Events, Leveraging Extensive Null Sampling) to combine the power of nonlinear machine learning with the rigorous false-positive control of traditional statistical inference. At each position of a sliding window, a random forest learns to discriminate event-locked activity from interleaved resting-state neural activity using multiscale temporal derivatives. Randomized feature ablation inverts slope polarity in held-out trials to map the random forest models' reliance on specific rising versus falling excursions across the time-frequency space. SafeLens then establishes an empirical null by running the same pipeline on separate resting-state recordings, training forests to discriminate rest from rest. This empirical null translates each channel's complex nonlinear resting dynamics into a model-matched noise floor on the map's linear reliance scale, allowing a single threshold to control the family-wise error rate against the channel's own background structure rather than a summary statistic of its baseline. When we injected simulated cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) into resting intracranial EEG recordings, SafeLens recovered ~2.5 times as many polarity-resolved deflections as trial-average thresholding and the closest data-driven method, maintaining its advantage under trial-to-trial variability while yielding ~5-11 times fewer false components, ~2-5 times lower mean boundary error, and superior single-trial latency tracking as a timing prior. In eight patients, CCEPs remained detectable above chance until 1,040 ms after stimulation, compared with 570 and 455 ms for those benchmarks. Together, these findings establish SafeLens as a novel solution for enabling nonlinear models to uncover subtle, trial-varying neural dynamics under strict statistical control.

ai.reason: Interpretable random-forest window analysis with empirical null control; a broadly useful, reproducible method for event-locked neural dynamics.
ai.summary: The authors introduce SafeLens, a nonlinear machine learning framework combining random forests with empirical null sampling to statistically control false positives when characterizing event-locked neural activity. In simulated corticocortical evoked potentials injected into intracranial EEG, SafeLens recovered ~2.5 times as many polarity-resolved deflections as trial-average thresholding and the closest data-driven method, with ~5-11 times fewer false components, and in eight patients detected CCEPs above chance until 1,040 ms after stimulation versus 570 and 455 ms for benchmarks.

papers.title: Synergistic contributions of periodic and aperiodic cortical activity to motor recovery prediction after stroke.
papers.abstract: Functional motor recovery in chronic stroke can be promoted by intensive exercise aided by neurotechnology, yet reliable physiological markers to predict recovery remain limited. Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used in clinical routines, but conventional band-power metrics conflate oscillatory (periodic) and broadband (aperiodic) activity, limiting their interpretability. Here, we tested whether EEG spectral profiles predict motor recovery in chronic stroke. Resting-state EEG (1 min) was recorded at admission and discharge using a portable system (N = 41) and parameterized with a spectral decomposition model. Parameters were examined in relation to motor improvement, as indexed by gain in a clinical score, and used to construct a prediction model. Ipsilesional periodic activity at the individual alpha frequency (IAF) significantly increased after rehabilitation (P = 0.024) and correlated with motor improvement (r = 0.39, P = 0.010). A stepwise regression model identified higher IAF peaks, steeper aperiodic slopes, and their interaction as predictors of recovery (Severe group: R 2 = 0.53, P = 0.003; balanced accuracy = 88%). The model outperformed a delta-alpha ratio-based approach commonly used in stroke prognosis. These findings indicate that the synergistic interaction between periodic and aperiodic activity provides a mechanistically meaningful and clinically relevant biomarker of residual plasticity, supporting individualized rehabilitation strategies in chronic stroke.

ai.summary: In 41 chronic stroke patients, resting-state EEG was spectrally decomposed into periodic and aperiodic components before and after rehabilitation. Ipsilesional alpha-frequency periodic activity increased with rehabilitation and a model combining higher individual alpha peaks, steeper aperiodic slopes, and their interaction predicted motor recovery (severe group R² = 0.53, balanced accuracy 88%), outperforming a delta-alpha ratio approach.

papers.title: Characterising cortical perturbation-recovery dynamics using TMS-EEG: The Brain Dynamic Toolbox
papers.abstract: Objective: To adapt dynamical measures used in computational and experimental perturbation models to human transcranial magnetic stimulation and electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and determine whether analysis of the extended post-stimulation trajectory reveals additional features of the cortical response to long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI). Methods: Single pulse and paired pulse LICI TMS-EEG responses from the bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex were re-analysed in 16 healthy adults. At the stimulation site, 75 single-pulse and 75 paired-pulse trials were delivered; paired pulses comprised conditioning and test stimuli separated by 100 ms. Responses from 20 frontocentral EEG channels were analysed from 50-950 ms following TMS using the open source Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox. Perturbative Integration Latency Index (PILI) indexed cortical resilience via response energy and recovery, Autocorrelation Function Width (ACFW) captured temporal memory, and Lyapunov Exponent (LE) indicated the dynamical stability. Linear mixed-effects models examined temporal, spectral, and time-frequency effects from the measured metrics. Results: LICI altered the temporal evolution of the dynamical measures. PILI distinguished conditions in the earliest post-stimulation window before converging, whereas ACFW differences persisted across a broader early interval. LE showed weaker and less consistent discrimination. Spectral effects were most evident for ACFW, while time-frequency analyses revealed later, frequency-specific LICI effects for PILI and ACFW but not LE. Conclusions: The extended post-stimulation trajectory revealed LICI-related differences in cortical resilience and temporal memory with distinct temporal and spectral profiles, while effects on dynamical stability were less consistent. Significance: The Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox provides a reproducible framework for quantifying perturbation-recovery dynamics in TMS-EEG and demonstrates that the extended perturbational response contains information about LICI not captured by discrete early response measures.

ai.reason: Open-source dynamical-metrics toolbox (autocorrelation width, Lyapunov) aligns with dynamical-system and interpretable-tool interests, though TMS-specific.
ai.summary: The study adapted dynamical measures from computational perturbation models to TMS-EEG data and applied them to analyze cortical perturbation-recovery dynamics in 16 healthy adults during long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI). It found that LICI altered the temporal evolution of dynamical measures: Perturbative Integration Latency Index distinguished conditions in the earliest post-stimulation window, Autocorrelation Function Width differences persisted across a broader early interval, and Lyapunov Exponent showed weaker discrimination, demonstrating that extended post-stimulation trajectories reveal additional features of cortical resilience and temporal memory.

papers.title: Slow power-envelope associations among brain, heart, and gut signals during sleep: an exploratory multivariate transfer entropy study.
papers.abstract: Sleep and the brain-gut axis both involve the coordinated regulation of the central nervous system (CNS), autonomic nervous system (ANS), and enteric nervous system. Although the role of the brain-gut axis in sleep regulation is increasingly recognized, the dynamic information flow and its directionality among the brain, heart, and gut systems during sleep remain unclear as statistical associations. In this study, based on overnight sleep data from 24 healthy subjects, we simultaneously collected occipital electroencephalogram (EEG), electrocardiogram, and bowel sound signals, constructed a multimodal physiological signal analysis framework, and employed a multivariate transfer entropy method based on non-uniform embedding and k-nearest neighbor estimation to systematically quantify directed statistical associations at the level of slow power envelope co-modulations among the brain, heart, and gut systems within the framework of sleep staging. The results reveal a consistent pattern of directed statistical associations: information transfer from heart to brain, brain to gut, and heart to gut consistently exceeds that in the reverse directions across all sleep stages. Sleep-stage dynamics further dissociate within-system from inter-system information flow: internal information exchange within the brain and gut intensifies with sleep depth and weakens during REM, whereas inter-system pathways show divergent stage-dependent patterns: heart-to-brain flow increases from light to deep sleep, while heart-to-gut and brain-to-gut flow are suppressed during deep sleep. At the frequency-band level, the brain, heart, and gut each exhibit dynamically reorganized source-receiver roles across sleep stages, with specific frequency bands contributing differentially to each inter-system pathway depending on sleep stage. This study identifies exploratory statistical patterns of directional information flow among the brain, heart, and gut systems during sleep, providing hypothesis-generating observations for future studies on sleep and multi-organ interactions. These directed associations do not establish anatomical pathways, causal regulation, or clinical biomarkers, and should be regarded as exploratory.

ai.reason: Sleep-stage-linked multivariate transfer entropy analysis of multimodal signals; relevant to sleep and signal-association methods though not staging per se.
ai.summary: Using overnight EEG, ECG, and bowel sound recordings from 24 healthy subjects, the study applied multivariate transfer entropy to quantify directed slow power-envelope associations among brain, heart, and gut across sleep stages. Information flow from heart to brain, brain to gut, and heart to gut consistently exceeded reverse directions, with sleep-stage-dependent dissociation of within- versus inter-system flow, presented as exploratory statistical patterns.

papers.title: Sleep and Neurodegeneration: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Early Detection and Personalized Care.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are increasingly recognized as both risk factors for and prodromal markers of neurodegenerative diseases. The glymphatic system provides a mechanistic basis for the bidirectional relationship between disrupted sleep and misfolded protein accumulation. Artificial intelligence (AI) applications, including automated sleep staging, wearable monitoring, and digital treatments, offer scalable tools for early detection and personalized sleep health promotion. This review examines current evidence linking sleep medicine, neurodegeneration, and AI.

ai.topic: AI for sleep staging and neurodegeneration early detection (review)
ai.reason: Review covering automated sleep staging and wearables for scalable monitoring; conceptually relevant though clinical/neurodegeneration focused rather than methodological.
ai.summary: This review examines evidence linking sleep disturbances, neurodegeneration, and artificial intelligence, covering the glymphatic system as a mechanistic basis for bidirectional sleep-proteinopathy relationships and AI applications such as automated sleep staging, wearable monitoring, and digital therapeutics for early detection and personalized care.

papers.title: Dissociable Oscillatory Alpha and Aperiodic Neural Dynamics Underlie Atypical Attentional Control in Children With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
papers.abstract: Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often have difficulty maintaining goal-directed attention when task-relevant and task-irrelevant information compete for processing resources. The present study investigated whether this difficulty reflects distinct abnormalities in demand-related attentional regulation and distractor-related neural responses. We recorded electroencephalography (EEG) signals from 45 children with ADHD and 45 typically developing (TD) children while they performed a visual detection task under low and high visual demands, with simultaneous task-irrelevant standard and deviant sounds. EEG power spectra were parameterized to separate oscillatory alpha activity from aperiodic activity, as putative indices of attentional regulation and cortical excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance, respectively. TD children showed adaptive demand-related alpha modulation, whereas children with ADHD showed an atypical alpha response pattern, including reduced frontal modulation and atypical posterior alpha enhancement; this demand-related group difference was observed in oscillatory alpha activity but not in aperiodic activity. In contrast, ADHD-related abnormalities in responses to auditory distractors were more clearly reflected in the aperiodic slope. Children with ADHD showed atypical distractor-related aperiodic modulation, suggesting reduced stability of neural background activity, potentially reflecting disrupted cortical E/I balance when irrelevant sounds had to be ignored. Furthermore, multivariate machine learning classification demonstrated that relying on these sensitive neural signatures yielded robust discrimination between children with ADHD and TD controls, with significant predictive performance emerging shortly after stimulus onset and sustaining throughout information processing. These findings suggest that oscillatory alpha activity and aperiodic neural dynamics show differential sensitivity to distinct attentional abnormalities in ADHD, with alpha oscillations primarily reflecting demand-related regulatory deficits and aperiodic activity primarily reflecting distractor-related neural instability.

ai.topic: Periodic vs aperiodic EEG spectral parameterization in ADHD
ai.reason: Highly transferable spectral decomposition (oscillatory vs aperiodic) method using EEG power spectra; useful for interpretable feature extraction, though application is pediatric ADHD, not sleep.
ai.summary: EEG from 45 children with ADHD and 45 typically developing children during a visual detection task was parameterized into oscillatory alpha and aperiodic components. Demand-related attentional differences appeared only in oscillatory alpha, whereas distractor-related abnormalities were reflected in the aperiodic slope, and multivariate machine learning classification based on these signatures robustly discriminated ADHD from controls.

papers.title: Clinical Validation of the New EEG Trend, Brain State of the Newborn, Against aEEG Interpretation.
papers.abstract: Previous studies have shown that the novel EEG trend, Brain State of the Newborn (BSN), is useful for monitoring recovery of electrocortical activity in high-risk newborns. Here, we validate the automatically computed BSN trend against visual amplitude-integrated EEG (aEEG) interpretation in asphyxiated hypothermia-treated infants. A total of 731 3-h aEEG epochs from 85 hypothermia-treated infants were randomized in order and scored independently by two clinical experts blinded for clinical data. First, we compared the BSN values to the aEEG scores at epoch level. Second, we assessed how the BSN trends align with aEEG scores in depicting electrocortical recovery. The BSN values showed robust differentiation between the experts' aEEG background scores (p ≤ 0.001 for all pairwise comparisons; effect size 1.0-6.5). Recovery of the BSN trend was also strongly correlated to the expert-defined aEEG recovery to continuous normal voltage (Spearman's ρ = 0.72, p < 0.001). The objective and fully automated BSN trend provides an effective, real-time complement to the visual aEEG interpretation. High BSN levels are reliable indicators of electrocortical recovery in hypothermia-treated infants. Future prospective studies are needed to establish evidence-based and context-sensitive clinical guidelines for the use of BSN in routine clinical care.

papers.title: Pediatric Sleep Medicine: Tailoring Artificial Intelligence Solutions for the Youngest Patients.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly relevant to pediatric sleep medicine, a field defined by complex physiologic signals, longitudinal behavioral data, time-intensive expert scoring, and uneven access to subspecialty care. Because sleep physiology, respiratory control, symptom expression, and monitoring tolerance change across development, pediatric practice cannot rely on adult-derived algorithms without age-specific training and validation. This review highlights the current evidence for AI-assisted obstructive sleep apnea screening and severity estimation, automated sleep staging, and more informative analysis of actigraphy and wearable signals. These tools may help reduce burden, support home and longitudinal monitoring, and streamline human review.

papers.title: Psychomotor vigilance is multidimensional: evidence from index network analysis, parameter review, and neuroimaging.
papers.abstract: The Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT) is widely used to assess vigilance, with interpretation shaped by experimental parameters, index definitions, and neurophysiological context. This review examines stimulus modality, task duration, and interstimulus interval, then considers the calculation and use of PVT indices. An exploratory network analysis of 15 indices in 678 participants examines a three-group descriptive framework comprising Stable, Overall, and Control indices. Electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetic resonance imaging findings relate vigilance to waking oscillations, EEG network stability, preceding sleep physiology, and functional brain connectivity. Multimodal assessment offers opportunities to refine vigilance monitoring in sleep medicine, fatigue research, and occupational settings such as aviation and shift work.

papers.title: Supporting the driver's perception cognition action loop using an embodied intelligent cockpit framework for explainable fatigue intervention.
papers.abstract: This study evaluated a driver-support framework combining multimodal fatigue detection, feature attribution, and state-specific auditory feedback during conditional automated driving. Forty licensed drivers completed three counterbalanced 20-min simulator conditions: nonverbal warnings, generic speech, and explanatory speech. A fixed detector used electroencephalography (EEG), eye tracking, and vehicle dynamics. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) selected a dominant cue, which a large language model translated into a spoken message. Fatigue labels were based on the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale and a 60-s vigilance task. Braking reaction time, standard deviation of lane position (SDLP), and time-to-collision (TTC) exposure were assessed during manual driving following takeover. Compared with generic speech, explanatory speech was associated with a 0.192-s shorter mean braking reaction time (95% confidence interval: -0.223 to -0.161 s; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001) and a 0.085-m lower mean SDLP (95% confidence interval: -0.108 to -0.062 m; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). The mean proportion of time with TTC < 1.5 s was 0.07 versus 0.10. Retrospective leave-one-subject-out evaluation yielded an area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve of 0.85. The explanatory warning package was associated with faster braking and more stable lane keeping than generic speech in this simulator study. Further studies should separate message content from acoustic properties and assess performance in independent driving settings.

papers.title: EEG emotion-recognition datasets for neuroarchitecture: an appraisal of openness, AI-readiness and ontology maturity.
papers.abstract: Neuroarchitecture studies how designed space shapes emotion, often with electroencephalography (EEG), and computational models that decode emotion from EEG must be trained on labelled recordings. Yet none of the widely shared EEG emotion datasets was recorded while people moved through designed spaces, and the few spatial recordings we found, all released since 2023, are single studies, each cited at most once. Researchers therefore borrow general emotion datasets, recorded from seated participants watching films, listening to music, playing games or conversing, and must decide whether each can be found, obtained and reused for transfer learning. This review contributes a reusable method for that decision and applies it. Following PRISMA 2020 with the dataset as the unit of analysis, two search passes identified 27 publicly obtainable datasets (22 in the first, 5 in the second), none designed for spatial research. A published codebook of 52 criteria defines three instruments: openness, judged against the FAIR principles with access class recorded separately; AI-readiness, the equally weighted mean of three sub-scores (label information, fit to standard tasks and alignment with other data), which describes usefulness as a transfer source; and ontology maturity, on five levels, which describes how far emotion labels can be mapped onto other vocabularies. Every identifier and access route was checked. Openness was weakest in Interoperability (2.044 against a FAIR composite of 2.857), and only 8 datasets were fully open. A dataset-level identifier was missing for 13 of 27 datasets (48.1%), and three widely used datasets could not be reached through their published routes at a re-check on 11 September 2026. AI-readiness averaged 2.684 on a 1.0-4.0 scale (median 2.60, range 2.10-3.33), and ontology levels concentrated at Level 3 (16 of 27), with none at Level 4 or 5. Openness and readiness were nearly unrelated (ρ = 0.08), whereas ontology level tracked readiness (ρ = 0.68), partly because both read the label structure. Open access alone is therefore a poor guide to reuse. The method, codebook and scripts are published so that researchers in fields without dedicated data can test the datasets they plan to reuse.

papers.title: Mapping brain networks underlying abstract perceptual decision formation and its EEG signatures
papers.abstract: Perceptual decisions have been proposed to involve a common mechanism of evidence accumulation operating across sensory modalities and motor contexts. In human EEG, the centroparietal positivity (CPP) tracks evidence accumulation in such a supramodal motor-independent manner, but its cortical sources are uncertain. Here we combined fMRI and EEG, acquired in separate sessions of the same supramodal change-detection paradigm, with individualized finite element head modeling to identify decision-related networks. A conjunction analysis across visual and auditory modalities and across motor and non-motor required tasks revealed consistent activation of bilateral postcentral, supramarginal, and superior parietal lobules, precentral gyrus, central operculum, middle frontal gyrus, and cerebellum. Forward modeling of fMRI-defined sources indicated that parietal-opercular regions were the dominant contributors to the response-locked and non-motor-required peak-locked CPP signal. These results implicate a network of brain areas in supramodal, motor-independent target-detection decisions, whose specific functional roles can be interrogated in more complex decision tasks in future.

papers.title: An Eyewear-Based EEG Interface for Temporal-Region Monitoring and Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Conventional electroencephalography (EEG) devices are often impractical for ambulatory settings due to their reliance on specialized hardware and expert operation. To address this, we developed a user-friendly eyewear-based EEG system featuring dry titanium electrodes positioned approximately 5 mm inferoposterior to the T7/T8 sites (near the ears), with metal nose pads serving as references. We evaluated the system across 103 recordings spanning five paradigms: alpha reactivity, blink-related transients, fatigue, attention, and video-elicited emotion. Following quality control, 93.2-100.0% of epochs were retained. The system demonstrated high sensitivity to ocular transients, showing significant amplitude increases during the blinking task. The emotion task yielded the most robust state-related features, with statistically significant differences in differential entropy across negative, neutral, and positive video categories, achieving balanced accuracies of 0.882 for two-class and 0.667 for three-class prediction. Despite challenges at the multiple testing correction stage, the alpha reactivity and fatigue contrast tasks were still noteworthy to some extent. The attention paradigm revealed a consistent increase in differential entropy during focused states, and the eyewear system outperformed the Muse headband in group-held-out classification. These findings provide strong evidence for the feasibility of temporal-region eyewear EEG acquisition, highlighting its potential applications in the real-world, particularly for emotion recognition.

papers.title: Repeated prefrontal transcranial direct current stimulation improves behavioral regulation and modulates resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in young adults with problematic smartphone use: a randomized sham-controlled longitudinal study.
papers.abstract: Problematic smartphone use (PSU) has emerged as an increasingly prevalent digital behavioral addiction among young adults and is associated with impaired executive control, excessive craving, and altered large-scale brain network organization. Although transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has demonstrated therapeutic potential for addictive disorders, its neurophysiological mechanisms in PSU remain insufficiently understood. This study investigated whether repeated prefrontal tDCS improves behavioral outcomes and reorganizes resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) microstate dynamics in young adults with PSU. Eighty participants meeting validated criteria for PSU were randomly assigned to receive active (n = 40) or sham (n = 40) tDCS. Active stimulation (2.0 mA, 20 min/session, three sessions/week for 12 weeks) targeted the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Behavioral outcomes included objectively recorded smartphone use, Smartphone Addiction Scale-Short Version scores, ecological momentary assessment craving, and work and social functioning. Resting-state EEG was recorded under eyes-closed and eyes-open conditions before and after intervention. Canonical EEG microstate temporal characteristics were analyzed using mixed repeated-measures analysis with false discovery rate correction. Compared with sham stimulation, active tDCS significantly reduced objectively measured smartphone use, craving intensity, and functional impairment while improving behavioral regulation. Neurophysiologically, active stimulation selectively reorganized resting-state brain dynamics. During eyes-closed recording, microstate C occurrence decreased whereas microstate D occurrence increased significantly. During eyes-open recording, both the occurrence and coverage of microstate B increased following active stimulation. No significant changes were observed in global explained variance, suggesting that repeated tDCS primarily modified the temporal organization rather than the spatial configuration of resting-state brain activity. Repeated prefrontal tDCS produced concurrent behavioral improvement and selective reorganization of resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in young adults with PSU. These findings provide preliminary evidence that repeated prefrontal tDCS is associated with concurrent behavioral changes and alterations in resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in young adults with PSU. Further confirmatory studies are needed to determine the clinical and mechanistic significance of these neurophysiological changes.

papers.title: Electroacupuncture alleviates TNBS-induced visceral pain and modulates cortical EEG rhythms in association with TREM1/DAP12 pathway inhibition: Enhanced effects with pharmacological TREM1 blockade.
papers.abstract: BackgroundVisceral pain in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) lacks effective therapies. Whether the TREM1/DAP12 pathway is associated with electroacupuncture (EA) analgesia and cortical EEG modulation remains unclear.ObjectiveTo determine if spinal TREM1/DAP12 is associated with EA's analgesic and neuromodulatory effects in TNBS-induced visceral pain.MethodsMale Sprague-Dawley rats with TNBS-induced colitis received EA (ST36/ST37), the TREM1 inhibitor Nangibotide, or their combination. Behaviors (PWT, CRD, DAI), spinal TREM1/DAP12, downstream inflammatory mediators, and microglial colocalization were evaluated. Cortical EEG was analyzed using normalized power spectral density (Normalized PSD, %).ResultsEA significantly alleviated visceral/referred hyperalgesia and reduced DAI scores (P < 0.05). TNBS upregulated spinal TREM1, DAP12, TNF-α, NLRP3, and TLR4 and increased TREM1/DAP12 microglial colocalization (P < 0.0001), all reversed by EA (P < 0.001). Nangibotide alone partially mimicked EA's effects, and their combination yielded greater analgesia and molecular suppression (P < 0.05). Normalized EEG analysis revealed that TNBS increased δ power (P < 0.0001) and reduced θ and β power (P < 0.001). Notably, EA and Nangibotide specifically reversed δ elevation and restored θ power (P<0.05) without altering β power (P > 0.05), with greater δ suppression than either treatment alone (P < 0.0001).ConclusionEA alleviates TNBS visceral pain and normalizes cortical δ/θ dysrhythmia, with these effects associated with suppression of microglial TREM1/DAP12 neuroinflammation. Pharmacological TREM1 blockade mimics and enhances EA's effects, supporting this pathway as a promising therapeutic target for visceral pain.

papers.title: Multiscale Neurodynamic Alterations in Major Depressive Disorder Revealed by Lempel-Ziv Complexity of Multi-Paradigm Resting-State EEG.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) abnormalities in major depressive disorder (MDD) have predominantly been examined through single-frequency band analyses or single-scale nonlinear measures, and largely within a single resting-state paradigm, which limits the characterization of regulatory interactions across temporal scales. In this study, we investigated dynamic transitions and integrative patterns of multiscale EEG activity in MDD across multiple resting-state paradigms, with a focus on characterizing alterations in multiscale neural dynamic organization. Based on multiscale Lempel-Ziv Complexity (LZC), we derived two classes of features quantifying the Scale-Dependent Variation Slope and the Cross-Scale Correlation Coefficient. Resting-state EEG from the MDD Patients and Healthy Controls EEG Data (MPHC) was analyzed under eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions to compare multiscale regulatory dynamics between patients with MDD and healthy controls. Patients with MDD showed impaired complexity transitions from low to high frequencies and disrupted delta-centered cross-scale integration. Distinct coupling reconfiguration patterns emerged across resting states, indicating a systemic imbalance in multiscale integrative organization. Classification models built from statistically selected features performed consistently across Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbor, and Decision Tree algorithms, reaching a maximum accuracy of 85.71% with a balanced sensitivity-specificity profile. Convergent results across models further suggested the preliminary discriminative value of the proposed features within the present dataset. These findings provide a preliminary multiscale neurodynamic framework for EEG characterization in MDD and suggest that cross-scale integration differences may provide a quantitative basis for characterizing multiscale EEG dynamics in depression.

papers.title: Clip-to-trial: EEG-based decoding network with long short-term self-attention for DRDS recognition.
papers.abstract: Dynamic random-dot stereograms (DRDS) elicit stereoscopic perception associated with high-level binocular visual processing, which can be decoded from EEG signals. However, existing EEG-based approaches predominantly rely on clip-level learning, leading to feature-label misalignment and limited modeling of trial-level spatiotemporal dependencies. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a clip-to-trial long short-term self-attention network (C2T-LSTSA) for EEG-based DRDS recognition. The proposed method first extracts discriminative spatiotemporal features from EEG clips using a multi-scale local feature extraction module. A trial-level feature reconstruction module is then introduced to explicitly map clip-level representations into semantically consistent trial-level features. Furthermore, a long short-term self-attention module is employed to jointly model local temporal dependencies within each reconstructed trial representation and global dependencies among multiple reconstructed trial representations derived from the same original EEG trial. Extensive experiments on three EEG datasets collected from strabismus patients demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches under both subject-dependent and subject-independent evaluation protocols, indicating its effectiveness and robustness for objective assessment of stereoscopic visual function. The reference datasets are available at https://github.com/YANGeeg/TJU-SRD-datasets and the code is at https://github.com/wu860898-design/C2T-LSTSA.

papers.title: Intraoperative electroencephalography burst suppression during endoscopic third ventriculostomy: Case report and implications for neuromonitoring.
papers.abstract: Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) is a common treatment for obstructive hydrocephalus. Intraoperative hemodynamic disturbances are well recognized. Their concurrent association with cortical suppression on electroencephalography (EEG), particularly burst suppression, has rarely been reported, and intraoperative EEG is seldom used during ETV. A 28-year-old woman underwent ETV for obstructive hydrocephalus secondary to a tectal glioma. Shortly after endoscope insertion and ventricular irrigation, she developed two successive episodes of severe tachycardia and an acute hypertensive crisis, each coinciding with an abrupt bilateral fall in fronto-temporal electrocortical activity with burst suppression on two-channel processed EEG. Irrigation was stopped and the endoscope was withdrawn. Systemic hemodynamics normalized within 15 min, whereas the EEG required 55 min to recover. The patient recovered to near-baseline within 4 h. This report represents only the second published case coupling an acute intraoperative hemodynamic surge with bilateral EEG burst suppression during ETV. Processed intraoperative EEG may be an additional early sign of an acute disturbance of cerebral function. Its added value remains unproven, since a hemodynamic emergency already mandates cessation of irrigation and endoscope withdrawal. Prospective evaluation with finer temporal sampling and raw-EEG recording is warranted.

papers.title: Nociceptive-evoked electroencephalography can predict inter-individual differences in high frequency induced sensitisation of central nociceptive pathways: A test-retest reliability study
papers.abstract: Evoked-EEG can capture changes in cortical responses during experimentally induced sensitised pain states. However, the test-retest reliability of such methods requires validation. The present study applied HFS across two identical sessions in the same individuals to assess the test-retest reliability of EEG dynamics evoked by a 128mN pin-prick stimulator and single-pulse electrical stimuli before and after HFS conditioning. The value of these features for reflecting individual differences in the development of hyperalgesia was also assessed. Results demonstrate poor-to-moderate test-retest reliability and relatively wide agreement at baseline for all features, with lateralised differences often present. This was further reduced when post-HFS changes were considered. -ERD assessed from contralateral central electrodes was significantly strengthened post-HFS for both electrical and pinprick stimuli, consistent with increased sensorimotor engagement in response to hyperalgesic and non-hyperalgesic stimuli. Notably, baseline -ERD was related to the subsequent time course of SHA development. Furthermore, whilst VP magnitude displayed a significant relationship with the general intensity of perceived pain, no specificity for SHA development was evident. Alternatively, {theta}-ERS captured a general habituation effect relative to variations in reported pain intensity between sessions for both stimuli modalities. These findings indicate that evoked EEG responses may be useful for investigating individual differences in the cortical processing of acute pain and the development time course of HFS-induced sensitivity yet may not possess sufficient test-retest reliability for interventional testing.

papers.title: Unexplained neurological deterioration after acute brain injury: A structured intensive care framework for targeted continuous electroencephalogram.
papers.abstract: Neurological deterioration after acute brain injury is common in the intensive care unit, yet its cause may remain uncertain when repeat imaging is stable or does not fully explain the examination. Delayed recognition of occult structural, vascular, systemic, metabolic, medication-related, or electrographic mechanisms may postpone time-sensitive treatment. We aimed to provide a structured bedside framework and define the role of targeted continuous electroencephalography (cEEG). We performed a narrative synthesis of evidence and consensus recommendations across aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, intracerebral hemorrhage, ischemic stroke, traumatic brain injury, and acute subdural hematoma, emphasizing bedside examination, repeat neuroimaging, vascular reassessment, systemic physiology, medication effects, and critical care electroencephalogram (EEG). Deterioration should first be confirmed as a true change and classified as explained, unexplained, disproportionate, or fluctuating/episodic. Evaluation should proceed in parallel: Correct reversible systemic and metabolic derangements, review sedative and analgesic exposure, and reassess structural or vascular complications. cEEG is most informative when deterioration remains unexplained after stabilization, exceeds the apparent imaging burden, fluctuates, follows a clinical seizure, or presents as delayed awakening. It can identify electrographic seizures, status epilepticus, and rhythmic or periodic patterns; however, a nonexplanatory recording neither establishes neurological stability nor excludes nonelectrographic secondary injury. A structured intensive care framework may reduce premature diagnostic closure and support timely, selective cEEG. Continuous EEG should complement, not replace, repeated clinical examination, neuroimaging, vascular evaluation, and correction of systemic physiology.

papers.title: E2I-Flow: EEG-to-Image Reconstruction via Wavelet-Temporal Cross-Attention and Conditional Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based visual decoding and reconstruction aims to recover visual information from non-invasive brain signals. But there are challenges due to the complex temporal-frequency characteristics of EEG signals and the difficulty of discrete denoising framework in mapping neural activity to meaningful visual representations. Here, we propose E2I-Flow, an EEG-to-image decoding and reconstruction framework that combines a novel EEG encoder for time-frequency representation learning from EEG features, and conditional flow matching for visual decoding. A stationary-wavelet frequency branch and a temporal-mixing branch are integrated through bidirectional cross-attention and adaptive fusion, with the resulting EEG representations aligned to ground-truth image embeddings using contrastive and mean-squared-error loss supervisions. The aligned EEG representation is then used as a condition for a Transformer-based flow-matching model to predict the corresponding visual embedding for image synthesis. Experimental results show strong zero-shot EEG-to-image retrieval and improved visual reconstruction performance, outperforming several state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: Resting-State EEG Graph Analysis Reveals Enhanced Alpha-Band Integration in High-IQ Individuals: The MENSA-Connect Project.
papers.abstract: To assess whether resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) connectivity differs between high-intelligence individuals (MENSA members) and controls using graph-theory metrics: clustering coefficient, characteristic path length, and small-worldness. Resting-state 64-channel EEG data were recorded in 29 MENSA participants and 20 controls. Functional connectivity was estimated using Lagged Linear Coherence across delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. Graph-theory measures were computed using sLORETA and the Brain Connectivity Toolbox. Between-group comparisons were performed using the Mann-Whitney U test; p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure, and effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals were calculated. Compared with controls, MENSA participants showed significantly lower characteristic path length in the alpha band (Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) critical value = 0.004), indicating greater global network integration. In the beta band, they showed a higher clustering coefficient (BH critical value = 0.008), reflecting greater local specialization; together with a higher characteristic path length (BH critical value = 0.013), suggesting reduced global communication. No significant group differences were observed in small-worldness across frequency bands. High-Intelligence Quotient (IQ) individuals show a frequency-dependent resting-state cortical organization, characterized by enhanced alpha-band integration and increased beta-band local specialization. These findings support a nuanced neural-efficiency model of intelligence without changes in small-world architecture. Given the cross-sectional and observational design, these findings should be regarded as associative rather than causal and require replication in larger, independent samples. These findings indicate frequency-specific differences in functional network organization, although their cognitive implications remain to be established.

papers.title: Matching Corticospinal and Cortical Excitability along the motor cortex: TMS-EMG-EEG study
papers.abstract: There is still no consensus on how to choose intensities for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). The resting motor threshold (RMT), the intensity needed to evoke muscle contractions in the contralateral limb muscles, is a robust muscle-specific index of corticospinal excitability. RMT from one of the hand muscles is commonly used as a reference for TMS neuromodulation interventions and TMS-electroencephalography (EEG) studies. However, it only provides an indirect measure of cortical excitability, and even for the primary motor cortex (M1), we do not understand how cortical and corticospinal excitability correspond to each other. Indeed, it remains unclear whether cortical responses to TMS follow similar location-dependent patterns along the M1, and whether subthreshold stimulation can reliably engage cortical circuits relevant to motor output. Combining TMS with electromyography (EMG) and EEG, TMS-EMG-EEG, enables simultaneous assessment of corticospinal and cortical excitability to answer these questions. We investigated how cortical excitability thresholds (CETs, measured with EEG), relate to corticospinal excitability thresholds (RMTs, measured with EMG) at the hand, arm, and leg hotspots along the M1 in 24 subjects. RMTs and CETs were strongly correlated, and both increased from hand to arm to leg. CETs were generally lower than RMTs, indicating that subthreshold stimulation was enough to evoke robust early TMS evoked potentials (TEPs). Within subjects, CETs differed from the corresponding RMTs at all three M1 hotspots, and this difference increased from hand to leg representations. The findings of the present study argue against using a default hand-muscle RMT to set cortical excitability dosage along the M1 and beyond. papers.title: In-person UCLA-PEERS® program for adolescents with autism spectrum disorder in Italy: study protocol for a pilot and feasibility randomized controlled trial with pragmatic features and exploratory EEG markers of treatment response.
papers.abstract: Adolescents with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Level 1 frequently experience persistent difficulties in peer relationships and social functioning that become more evident as social demands increase. Group-based social skills trainings represent a key evidence-based intervention for this population, yet its availability in routine clinical services is still limited. The Program for the Education and Enrichment of Relational Skills (PEERS®) is one of the most empirically supported interventions for autistic adolescents. In Italy, telemedicine delivery has shown promising results, but the effectiveness and implementation of the in-person format in real-world services have not yet been evaluated. In addition, predictors of individual response to psychosocial interventions remain largely unknown. This study is designed as a two-arm pilot and feasibility randomized controlled trial incorporating pragmatic features, including delivery within a routine tertiary clinical service, comparison with Treatment as Usual (TAU), and allowance for ongoing concomitant clinical, educational, and pharmacological treatments. It will compare the in-person Italian adaptation of UCLA PEERS® with Treatment as Usual (TAU) at IRCCS Fondazione Stella Maris (Pisa, Italy). Thirty-six adolescents aged 11-13 years with ASD (DSM-5-TR) and Full-Scale IQ >85 will be assessed at baseline (T0) and after the 16-week intervention (T1). Randomization will use block allocation with allocation concealment until completion of baseline assessments; outcome assessors and independent ADOS-BOSCC video coders will remain blind to group assignment. The intervention includes sixteen weekly 90-minute group sessions delivered by certified providers, with parallel caregiver sessions and structured teacher contacts to promote generalization. The primary focus of this pilot trial is feasibility, assessed through recruitment, retention, session attendance, and treatment fidelity. Clinical outcomes will be examined exploratorily to provide preliminary estimates of treatment effects. The QSQ-R will serve as the prespecified principal clinical outcome for estimating change in social functioning from baseline to T1. Parent- and adolescent-report versions will be analyzed separately, considering the Social Initiative and Social Reciprocity dimensions as distinct outcomes rather than deriving a composite total score. Key secondary outcomes include social knowledge (TASSK-R), autism-related social responsiveness (SRS-2), social motivation (SSDS), social anxiety (SAS), and observational change in social-communication behaviors (ADOS-BOSCC). Emotional-behavioral functioning (CBCL; YSR) will be explored as additional secondary outcomes. Baseline electroencephalography (EEG) recorded during a gesture-word integration task will be used to derive the N400 congruency effect and to explore whether individual differences in this measure are associated with treatment response. As a pilot and feasibility trial, the study is not powered for definitive efficacy testing and will estimate feasibility, acceptability, fidelity, and preliminary effect sizes to inform future multicenter trials. This study will provide the first evaluation of in-person PEERS® in the Italian clinical context and test the generalizability of previous telemedicine findings in routine care. The integration of clinical and behavioral outcomes may contribute to mechanism-informed, personalized psychosocial interventions for autistic adolescents and guide the design of future confirmatory studies. papers.title: Reducing the Risk of Gradient Induced EEG Hardware Heating During Simultaneous EEG-fMRI
papers.abstract: Simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional MRI (fMRI) has the potential to provide a more complete characterisation of brain function. Acquiring these data simultaneously requires the EEG hardware to be MR safe, since the EEG cap, amplifiers and powerpacks must be located within the MR environment. Placing them in this environment exposes them to both static and varying (radiofrequency (RF) and gradient) magnetic fields, presenting a potential heating risk. Previous studies have typically positioned the amplifiers and powerpacks outside of the bore, meaning that this risk is largely limited to the EEG cap. However, current guidelines recommend positioning the amplifiers within the bore. This reduces the distance between the EEG electrodes and amplifier, improving EEG signal quality and reducing risks of RF heating at the electrodes, but presents a potential heating risk for the amplifiers and powerpacks from the varying magnetic field gradients. In this study, we demonstrate that placing the amplifiers and powerpacks in the bore presents a significant heating risk, both at 7T and 3T. At 7T, we show that EPI sequences with a slew rate of at least 88 T/m/s resulted in significant heating of the EEG amplifiers. This heating effect could be negated by reducing the slew rate to 61 T/m/s. At 3T, we replicate the EEG amplifier heating and show that an alternative approach to reducing the gradient slew rates experience by the hardware is to increase the distance between the EEG amplifier/powerpacks and the isocentre of the magnet. Increasing the distance between the EEG hardware and MR isocentre by 30 cm mitigates the heating risk to the amplifiers and powerpacks, regardless of sequence parameters (e.g., slew rate). Therefore, whilst reducing the distance between the electrodes and amplifiers may improve EEG signal quality and reduce the potential for electrode RF heating, we show that risk of heating of hardware by gradient switching is greatly increased. This is particularly important to consider with the faster gradient slew rates available on modern MRI scanners, desired to increase spatial resolution. Experimenters must make careful decisions about hardware placement to ensure that the EEG-fMRI setup they use is safe, taking account of the varying risks that are posed by different approaches.

papers.title: Multimodal characterization of putative pan-inhibitory viral constructs in macaque monkeys
papers.abstract: Transgenic approaches and validated viral vector toolboxes have advanced our understanding of how inhibitory neurons shape cognition and motor control in mice and other rodents. However, such advances have been elusive in non-human primates (NHPs). While many studies demonstrate expression of reporter proteins, few studies have provided clear quantitative evidence of whether these viral constructs can be reliably used for assessment of in vivo and in vitro function in primates, which, in turn, has hindered widespread adoption by NHP researchers. Here, we characterize putative pan-inhibitory cell targeting vectors engineered with regions from the Dlx5-6 intergenic domain. Pan-inhibitory viral vectors are attractive because they enable ground-truth optotagging and modulation of multiple inhibitory subtypes in the same animal and, when combined with machine learning approaches, enable cell-type classifiers for NHPs. We combined in vivo anesthetized electrophysiological recordings, in vitro slice electrophysiology, and immunohistochemistry across seven rhesus macaque monkeys to assess the specificity, completeness and efficacy of three constructs in multiple sensory and higher-order association cortices. The vectors reliably restricted transgene expression to inhibitory neurons (81-97%). However, of the local GABAergic neurons only 32-64% expressed the transgene, depending on the construct. This incompleteness arose in part from uneven coverage across subtypes, with strong transgene expression in parvalbumin-positive interneurons (~60-90%), sparse expression in calbindin-positive interneurons (~1-7%), and near-complete avoidance of calretinin-positive interneurons. A construct pairing DLX2.0 with ChrimsonR was excellent for in vivo optotagging, while h56D paired with bReaChES most effectively suppressed neural activity in vivo. In the slice, activating terminals of transgene-expressing neurons optically evoked inhibitory currents in coupled pyramidal neurons confirming transsynaptic functionality of these constructs and their use for inhibitory circuit-specific synaptic assessments and manipulation. Collectively, the results provide rigorous functional characterization, and quantitative guidance for NHP researchers seeking to deploy GABAergic cell-type-specific tools in their experiments.

papers.title: Disambiguation of two-tone images aligns object representations in the EEG
papers.abstract: Electrophysiological responses to visual objects carry information about stimulus identity and semantic category, but it remains difficult to know whether such information represents conceptual knowledge or merely regularities in physical image features. Here, we presented two-tone images before and after disambiguation via corresponding photographs to seventeen healthy participants while recording EEG to dissociate the learned image concept from its physical properties. After disambiguation, EEG responses to learned two-tone images became more similar to the responses of their photo counterparts. This effect emerged approximately 100 ms after stimulus onset and peaked at 350 ms. However, we found no evidence for a generalization of the response pattern to the stimulus semantic category. Furthermore, alignment to the photo counterparts was only detectable after explicit visual disambiguation rather than spontaneous recognition. Together, these findings indicate that EEG can capture specific learned conceptual modulations of responses to visually degraded stimuli, while also showing that low-level visual properties dominate the representational structure.
